items.finding: The review states that the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for NIR and MIR measurements of aqueous solutions, making tempered sample holders necessary.
items.how_it_applies: Since the product is aqueous and temperature varies during production, temperature should be recorded alongside the NIR spectra and included as a calibration variable or used to select/segment calibration data. A temperature sensor at the probe location is a reasonable auxiliary measurement to test whether it improves model robustness.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The quote concerns aqueous solutions in laboratory NIR/MIR with tempered sample holders, not an opaque concentrated dairy product measured in-line; the magnitude of the temperature effect on this matrix is unknown.

citation.quote: Additionally, the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, which makes tempered sample holders necessary [29].
citation.label: E01 ¶12

items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest combination approach, where variables from different sources are concatenated one after the other into a new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the planned low-level fusion of synchronised NIR and Raman spectra into one augmented matrix for PLS regression as an established, simple fusion scheme. The comparison experiment can implement exactly this concatenation and benchmark it against single-method models.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The review describes the method generically; it does not state performance gains for NIR+Raman fusion of a concentrated dairy product, and synchronisation quality in-line is not addressed.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E02 ¶31

items.finding: A Raman and FT-IR food analytical study cited in the review showed that in some situations instrument complementarity alone was not sufficient to improve the prediction of several CQAs.
items.how_it_applies: This is a reason to keep the planned acceptance criterion: the fused model must beat the best single-method model on held-out runs before the extra Raman instrument is justified. The experiment should explicitly test whether the second method adds predictive value for fat and protein.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study used Raman with FT-IR on food samples, not NIR with Raman on an opaque concentrated milk product in-line, so the outcome may differ.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36

items.finding: The review states that before fusing data from multiple sources it is essential to evaluate each dataset's contribution to the model and its complementarity.
items.how_it_applies: The comparison experiment should include a step assessing each method's individual contribution and complementarity before building the fused model, e.g. by comparing single-method PLS models and checking which wavelengths/Raman shifts carry fat and protein information.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a general methodological recommendation from a review, not a demonstrated result for this product or instrument pair.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
citation.label: E02 ¶82

items.finding: In the FT-IR and Raman study, concentrations as well as ionic strength and temperature were deliberately varied to obtain a robust model.
items.how_it_applies: This suggests a practical design choice for the calibration experiment: deliberately vary product temperature (and composition) across expected production conditions so the model becomes robust to the temperature and texture variations mentioned in the enquiry.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The study concerns acids and ionic strength in a lithium recycling extraction, a very different matrix from concentrated milk, so the transferable point is the design principle, not the results.

citation.quote: The concentrations of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid as well as the ionic strength and temperature were varied to obtain a robust model.
citation.label: E03 ¶19

items.finding: The study notes that in-line methods require maintenance such as calibration and handling of sensor drift and aging, which can be addressed by checking the baseline in each cycle and monitoring drift.
items.how_it_applies: This supports retaining laboratory checks and adding routine baseline/drift monitoring in the concept, since in-line spectroscopy performance can degrade over time. The assessment should plan periodic lab reference sampling to verify the in-line calibration.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The recommendation comes from a fixed-probe liquid-liquid extraction process with pure-component phases available for baseline checks; a continuous dairy line may not offer comparable reference phases.

citation.quote: Potential typical drawbacks of any in-line method are maintenance efforts like calibration, and actions to sensor drift and aging could be easily overcome by checking the baseline in each cycle of pure component phases of process operation and monitoring any drift in order to be able to react.
citation.label: E03 ¶72
